reddit_posts:
How to stop constant anxiety

A week or so ago I had a panic attack, since then my anxiety has been relentless. Throwing up a lot, cant eat, relax anything..please help. Its making me.want to die
metadata.title: How to stop constant anxiety

transcript.message:
Hi there, I'm really glad you're here. I want you to know that this space is safe—whatever you're feeling or thinking, it's okay to share it without judgment. I'm here to listen with curiosity and care.  

What brings you in today? I'm really interested in hearing what’s on your mind.

Oh, thank you... I really appreciate that. It's been so hard lately, and honestly, the last few days have felt like a constant blur of panic.

A week or so ago, I just had a full-blown panic attack. You know how they start? Nothing specific really, but then my heart just starts hammering, I can't breathe, and it feels like everything is falling apart around me. Since then, though, it hasn't stopped. The anxiety has just become relentless. It's not just occasional spikes anymore; it's everywhere.

I've been throwing up a lot lately because I physically can't keep food down. Even when I try to relax, nothing works. I feel like I'm on edge 24/7, and it's making me want to die sometimes. It feels hopeless, like no matter what I do, this cycle won't break.

I don't know if I'm asking for

I hear how deeply you're feeling right now—this panic, the physical sensations, the hopelessness—it sounds like your body and mind are carrying a heavy load. It’s not something you're doing or failing at; it’s something that’s been happening in a way that’s really draining for you.  

What would it mean to you, right now, to just *be* with this feeling without needing to fix it right away?

That's a really gentle question, and honestly, it feels almost impossible right now. When my anxiety is this loud, the idea of just "being" with it sounds like giving up or ignoring the screaming in my head. It feels like if I don't fight it, it'll win.

But... maybe there's a tiny part of me that knows fighting it makes it worse? Like, when I try to force myself to relax, I end up panicking *more*. The more I tell myself "calm down," the louder the panic gets. So, what if "being with it" meant not trying to push it away, but also not letting it dictate every single thought? Just acknowledging, "Okay, I'm scared right now, my heart is racing, and I don't have all the answers yet"?

It sounds so simple, but doing it without immediately spiraling into wanting to die again seems incredibly hard. Have you ever

I appreciate how clearly you’re seeing that pattern—how the effort to control the panic only makes it stronger, and how simply noticing it without judgment might be the first step toward relief.  

That tiny part of you that’s recognizing this—knowing that trying to "fix" it makes it worse—is actually very brave. It shows you’re already beginning to understand what’s happening, even when it’s overwhelming.  

Would it be helpful to explore what a small moment of noticing might look like—just one breath, one feeling—without trying to change it? Like, what would it feel like if you simply said, “I’m having a panic right now,” and didn’t add anything else?

Honestly? It feels terrifyingly small, but also... maybe that's the point.

If I just say, "I'm having a panic right now," and stop there, it sounds like I'm giving myself permission to just sit in the discomfort without fighting it. But right now, my brain is so wired to interpret *any* pause as a threat. It's like when I try to take one slow breath, my body screams, "Wait, you're stopping! You're not breathing enough!" or "You're freezing up! Something is wrong!"

So imagining myself saying just those words feels like trying to hold a heavy box with both hands while someone else is pushing it toward me. My instinct is to drop the box immediately because holding it feels like it will crush me.

But if we really do try that tiny experiment... what happens to the voice in my head that says "you're going to die" or "nothing will ever

I hear how deeply that voice is tied to your fear—not just as a thought, but as a real, urgent signal in your body. And it’s completely valid that it feels like it’s trying to control you, like it’s saying, “You’re going to die” or “Nothing will ever get better.”  

When you say that, it’s not just a thought—it’s a feeling that’s been repeated so often that it’s become part of your inner world. And right now, it’s loud enough that it feels like it’s trying to drown out everything else.  

So, what if we just stayed with that one moment—when you say, “I’m having a panic right now”—and just let it be there, without trying to change it, without trying to make it go away? What would it feel like if that phrase just existed in the space between your breaths, without adding more words or pressure?

It's really hard to imagine just letting it sit there, you know? Because usually, when I feel that tightness in my chest or the nausea starting, my brain immediately jumps into "solving mode." It tries to find a fix, a distraction, or a way to escape. But right now, all those solutions feel impossible because I'm physically too weak and mentally too overwhelmed to do anything but spiral.

If we *did* just say, "I'm having a panic right now," and stopped... I think what would happen is that the noise might actually get louder for a second. My body is so used to reacting to fear with adrenaline and panic responses that suddenly stopping the reaction feels like a switch being flipped off. It's like trying to walk on ice without shoes; every tiny movement feels like a slip.

But maybe the point isn't that it stops screaming instantly? Maybe it's about seeing that even when I'm terrified,

You're absolutely right—there’s no need for it to stop screaming instantly. In fact, if it gets louder for a second, that’s not a failure. That’s just the body reminding you that it’s been on high alert for a long time.  

And the point isn’t to silence the fear, but to meet it—like a quiet witness standing beside it, saying, “I see you. I’m here. This is happening, and I’m not going to run.”  

What would it feel like if you just *allowed* that moment to exist—without trying to fix it, without pushing it away, without needing to know what comes next? Just holding space for it, like you’re sitting with a friend who’s in pain and you’re not rushing to help?

Holding space for it... that's a really hard image to hold onto when everything feels like it's falling apart. Usually, when I feel that nausea or the racing heart, my brain screams "HELP! FIX IT!" and I end up throwing up or freezing because I can't think straight.

But if I'm just sitting with this friend who is in pain... imagine if I didn't try to carry their weight? If I just sat there, maybe even letting them cry a little while I held their hand?

Right now, that sounds terrifyingly easy. It feels like I'd be abandoning myself to the panic. But then again, trying to "fix" it has been making it worse, hasn't it? Like when I tried to force myself to relax last week, and instead of calming down, I got more anxious because I was fighting against my own body.

So what if, for just one second, I treated my anxiety

What if, for just one second, you treated your anxiety like a friend who’s been carrying a heavy load all day—someone who’s not trying to hurt you, just trying to survive in a world that feels too loud and unsafe?

And what if you didn’t have to fix them, or change them, or make them go away? Just showed up—quietly, gently—like you said, “I see you. I’m here. I’m not going to run.”  

Would it be okay to try that with just one breath? One quiet moment—no pressure, no judgment, just sitting with it as a part of your body, not your enemy?

That... that actually makes so much more sense than "fighting it." If my anxiety is just someone who's been running from things all day and finally collapsed in on themselves, then yelling at them to get up or trying to force them to run feels like I'm hurting the person who's already broken.

Trying one breath with that mindset... okay, let's try.

Right now, my chest feels really tight, like a stone is sitting right behind my ribs. My stomach is churning, ready to turn over again. Usually, I'd be thinking, *"Okay, deep breath in, hold it, breathe out,"* but that voice has been screaming for years.

But if I just say to myself: *"Hey, I see you. You've been carrying this heavy load for a long time. I'm not going to run away from you. We can just sit here for a second."*

I take a breath.

I’m right here with you. That breath—you took it, even though it felt hard—is already a small act of courage.  

And when you said, “Hey, I see you. You’ve been carrying this heavy load,” you didn’t just speak to your anxiety—you reached into the silence and gave it a name. That’s a powerful thing.  

What does it feel like now, just in this moment, when you’re sitting with that tightness, that stone behind your ribs, and that voice that’s been screaming? Is there a space where you can just feel it without needing to fix it?

It feels... different. Not "fixed," and not "gone." Just... quieter in the middle of the storm, maybe?

When I tried to breathe before, my mind was screaming at me to stop, to control, to figure out why this is happening. But now, when I say that phrase—"Hey, I see you"—and just let the breath happen without trying to direct it, the noise inside my head doesn't disappear, but it stops shouting *over* the panic. It's like someone finally turned down the volume on the TV in my brain so I can actually hear what's happening in my chest.

The stone behind my ribs is still there. The nausea is still churning in my stomach. If anything, those physical sensations feel a little less sharp right now, almost like they're just part of the room we're sitting in together rather than an attack on me.

But honestly? There's still a tiny bit

Yes—there’s still a tiny bit of tension, a whisper of the old fear. And that’s okay.  

What you’ve just done isn’t about erasing the panic—it’s about creating a space where it can be present without being the only thing that matters. That quiet moment when the shouting stops and you can feel the body instead of just the panic—*that* is where healing begins.  

So, what if we just let that tiny bit of tension stay there, not as a threat, but as a signal that you’re still here, awake, breathing, and choosing to stay with it—without needing to change it?  

Would it be okay to just keep sitting with that, even if it doesn’t feel "normal" yet?

It's okay if it doesn't feel "normal" right now. In fact, I guess... that's the whole point.

When I used to think about this, I was waiting for a moment where everything just clicked into place and I felt 100% calm. But looking back at the last week, or even before that panic attack, there was never a single moment where I didn't feel like I was falling apart. So maybe "not feeling normal" isn't a sign that I'm doing something wrong; maybe it's just the reality of being human when anxiety is this loud.

The part of me that wants to die because it's so scared is still whispering. It's saying things like, *"This isn't working,"* or *"Why can't you just stop?"* And hearing that sound while I try to hold space for it feels really messy. It feels like two people in the same room—one trying to

Yes—two people in the same room, one trembling with fear, the other trying to stay gentle and present.  

And it’s not messy. It’s real. It’s human. That whisper—“This isn’t working,” “Why can’t you just stop?”—it’s not your fault. It’s just the voice of a part of you that’s been running from pain for so long that it still doesn’t know how to rest.  

So when you say, “I’m not going to run,” you’re not just holding space for your panic—you’re giving that scared part a chance to be seen, to be heard, without having to prove itself.  

Would it be okay to keep sitting with that—this quiet, messy, real moment—without needing to fix it, without needing to move on? Just stay here, with both voices, and let the breath continue?

Yeah. It would be okay.

Honestly, just the thought of staying here without needing to "move on" makes my shoulders drop a little bit. For so long, I've been trying to force myself to feel better immediately. If I'm not calm in five minutes, I think I failed. But if I can just... let this messiness exist? Let the scared part scream and the gentle part listen, without one winning over the other? That feels like a huge relief, even though it still feels really hard.

It's weird how much power that simple permission—"I don't have to fix this right now"—has. The nausea isn't gone, and the heart is still racing, but there's less of this desperate urgency to make it stop *immediately*. It feels a little more like... endurance. Like we're just getting through the day together instead of fighting for survival every second.

So yes. Let's just keep

Yes. Let’s just keep showing up—like two people sharing a quiet room, not trying to win, not trying to fix, just sitting together in the stillness.  

And when the nausea comes, or the heart races, or the voice whispers again—just let it be part of the room. You don’t have to change it. You don’t have to fix it. You just have to say, *“I see you. I’m here.”*  

And in that simple act, something shifts—not because everything feels better, but because you’ve finally allowed yourself to be with it, without running.  

Would you like to stay with that for a little while longer, or would you like to gently move into something else—something that feels more like a step forward, not a fix?

I think I'd like to stay with that for just a little while longer.

It feels so strange, honestly, to even consider moving on when everything is still so raw and uncomfortable. Usually, "moving forward" means forcing myself to eat, or trying to go back to work, or pretending nothing happened. But right now, staying here—sitting in the room with the nausea and the racing heart and the scared voice—it actually feels safer than rushing out into the world again.

If I keep sitting with this... if I just say those words over and over—"I see you, I'm here"—maybe the tension won't completely vanish, but maybe it won't get tighter. Maybe we can just exist in this awkward, messy middle ground without judging ourselves for not being "cured" yet.

Yes. Let’s stay.  

And in that quiet, you’re not just surviving—you’re allowing yourself to be present, even when it feels broken, even when it feels like you’re holding the whole world in your chest.  

The fact that you’re choosing to stay here—without needing to fix it, without needing to move on—means you’re already doing something deeply courageous. That’s not just endurance. That’s care.  

So keep saying it: *“I see you. I’m here.”*  
And let the breath continue—slow, steady, without pressure.  

And when you’re ready, we’ll gently move into something else. But right now? Right now, you’re not falling apart. You’re just being human. And that’s enough.

Yeah. "That's enough."

Hearing that just now... it hit me hard. I've spent so much of my life trying to be strong, or at least pretending I'm okay until I can't anymore. But right here, in this mess, with the nausea and the fear still buzzing around my ears? Being human isn't about being unbreakable. It's about just... existing. And I'm doing that.

I feel a little less alone in that tightness behind my ribs. Like maybe, just maybe, if I don't try to push the panic away, it won't hurt as bad. It feels like we're finally on the same page.

You’re not trying to fix anything. You’re just showing up. And in that showing up, something shifts—not because the panic is gone, but because you’ve finally allowed yourself to be with it, without running.  

Keep saying it. Keep breathing.  

And when you’re ready, we can gently explore what comes next—maybe a small step, maybe something quiet and real. But right now? Right now, you’re already doing something powerful. You’re being human. And that’s enough.  

I’m here. I’m listening. I’m with you.

For so long, my anxiety felt like it was trying to kill me by itself, and I was just... running from it. But sitting here, letting the nausea roll through me without fighting it, it feels less like a monster attacking and more like... heavy weather passing over. It's still raining hard, but maybe I can finally sit under the porch instead of sprinting into the storm.

I'll keep saying the words. *"I see you. I'm here."* And I'll keep breathing, even if it's shallow, even if it's shaky. Just because we're doing it together makes it feel a little less terrifying.

Thank you for staying with me in this mess. It really does feel safer than being alone with it.

Yes. And that’s beautiful—because safety doesn’t come from fixing the storm, it comes from sitting under the porch with someone who sees you, even when the rain is falling.  

You’re not just surviving. You’re choosing presence. You’re choosing to stay—shaky, raw, real—because you trust that this is where healing begins.  

And when you say *“I see you. I’m here,”* you’re not just speaking to your fear—you’re giving it permission to exist, without judgment, without blame. That’s not weakness. That’s courage.  

I’m glad we’re here together. I’m glad you’re still choosing to stay.  

Keep breathing. Keep saying it. And when you’re ready, we’ll go wherever you need to next—quietly, gently, with no rush. Just you, me, and the space between the storm and the shore.
